tasks.q: Match each flowchart symbol to what it represents.
tasks.fb: These four cover almost every flowchart you will draw or read.

tasks.q: Which symbol has two arrows leaving it?
a: The diamond, because a decision has a yes path and a no path
tasks.fb: Every decision splits the flow in two.

tasks.q: A flowchart reads: input n, is n greater than 10, if yes output 'big', if no output 'small'. What does an input of 7 produce?
tasks.fb: 7 is not greater than 10, so the no path is taken.

tasks.q: A flowchart has an arrow going back to an earlier box. What does that show?
tasks.fb: Loops in flowcharts are drawn as arrows going back up.

tasks.q: Put these boxes into the order a grading flowchart would use.
tasks.fb: Test the highest boundary first, or a distinction is reported as a merit.

tasks.q: Why must the highest grade be tested first?
a: Otherwise a mark of 80 would match the lower condition and be given the wrong grade
Because diamonds must be in order
tasks.fb: Order of conditions is a classic source of logic errors.

tasks.q: Put these boxes into the order for a flowchart that totals ten numbers.
steps: Set the total to 0 and the count to 0
Add it to the total and add 1 to the count
tasks.fb: The decision sends the flow back to the input box until the count reaches ten.

tasks.q: What happens if the loop's decision can never be true?
a: The program never stops: an infinite loop
tasks.fb: Always check the condition can eventually be met.

tasks.q: When is a flowchart the better choice?
a: When explaining the shape of an algorithm to someone who does not program
When the algorithm is 500 lines long
tasks.fb: Pictures are good for structure and poor for length.

a: A flowchart and pseudocode can describe exactly the same algorithm
tasks.fb: They are two notations for the same thing.

stations.name: Drawing a flowchart in the exam

tasks.q: Which of these would lose marks in a flowchart question? Select all that apply.
opts: Using a rectangle for a decision
Leaving the arrows from a diamond unlabelled
A path that never reaches a stop
correct: Using a rectangle for a decision
Leaving the arrows from a diamond unlabelled
A path that never reaches a stop
tasks.fb: Neatness is not marked; correct symbols and complete paths are.

tasks.q: A flowchart's decision has only one arrow leaving it. What is wrong?
a: A decision must have both a true and a false path
tasks.fb: Otherwise there is no way through when the condition is false.

tasks.q: Put the boxes of the ticket machine flowchart into order.
tasks.fb: Start, input, decide, set, output, stop: the shape of most short flowcharts.

tasks.q: Which flowchart symbol would each step use?
tasks.fb: Getting the symbol right is where the marks are.

info.title: Older than software
info.text: Flowcharts were used to plan industrial processes in the 1920s, long before they were used for programs.

info.title: Standard shapes
info.text: The symbols are set out in an international standard, which is why a flowchart drawn in one country is readable in another.

info.title: Why diamonds
info.text: The diamond was chosen because two arrows can leave it cleanly, one from each side.

info.title: Too big to draw
info.text: Real programs are far too large to flowchart. They are used for the tricky part, not the whole thing.

info.title: Drawing tools
info.text: Any diagram tool will do, and drawing one by hand on paper is perfectly acceptable in the exam.

info.title: Exam tip
info.text: Read a flowchart with a specific input and follow the arrows with your finger. Most reading errors come from skipping a branch.
